    {
      "startEvent":89,"endEvent":90,"contextStartEvent":43,"contextEndEvent":113,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"out of nothing, nothing comes.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"The maxim summarizes the causal premise explicitly stated at E95–E101. E64–E88 explain its intended application to the origin of physical reality and invoke scientific commitment. The premise is contestable, but the maxim is part of an articulated argument rather than an independent replacement for one.",
      "protectionExplanation":"No objection is ruled out regardless of merits. A subsequently discusses objections to the beginning and causal reasoning at E646–E680.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A concise statement of a causal principle within a longer cosmological argument."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":165,"endEvent":166,"contextStartEvent":163,"contextEndEvent":208,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"Nothing is forbidden. Everything is permitted.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E168–E190 provide the intended reasoning: goal-relative recommendations allegedly cannot categorically condemn individual or societal wrongdoing. Later E1224–E1239 distinguish moral foundations from moral knowledge. The sweeping wording exceeds ordinary permissions, but it summarizes an argument actually supplied.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The maxim itself does not exclude criticism. The separate claim about a sound moral sense at E191 warrants its own protection assessment.",
      "emotionalDevices":["fear"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A dramatic shorthand for the alleged absence of binding, opinion-independent prohibitions, not a prediction that atheists will behave criminally."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":191,"endEvent":191,"contextStartEvent":183,"contextEndEvent":208,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"Anyone with a sound moral sense knows that this cannot be right.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"yes","protection":"yes",
      "supportExplanation":"E185–E190 supply disturbing examples. This affirmation then treats a sound person's reaction as settling whether morality is objectively binding, without separating condemnation of those acts from acceptance of A's account of moral foundations.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The universal formulation makes rejection of the conclusion evidence of an unsound moral sense. That is a local protective move, even though A gives additional moral arguments and later explicitly denies accusing atheists of criminal inclinations at E1191–E1203.",
      "emotionalDevices":["shame","identity"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"An appeal to widely shared moral experience intended as evidence, rather than a diagnosis of every person who rejects theism."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":257,"endEvent":258,"contextStartEvent":209,"contextEndEvent":272,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"The simple fact is that there just is no plausible naturalistic explanation of these facts",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E223–E253 identify three proposed historical facts and supporting scholarly testimony; E254–E256 name rejected alternatives. The assessment is sweeping and not exhaustive, but it summarizes an offered historical inference. Later E1248–E1260 name sources and historical criteria.",
      "protectionExplanation":"Calling alternatives implausible does not by itself immunize the explanation. A proposes historical examination and comparison, including at E1275–E1277.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A condensed inference to what A regards as the best historical explanation, with contestable claims about scholarly agreement."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":284,"endEvent":286,"contextStartEvent":273,"contextEndEvent":290,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"We mustn't so concentrate on the arguments that we fail to hear the inner voice of God speaking to our hearts.",
      "form":"no","substitution":"unclear","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E274–E283 propose immediate experience as another route to knowledge. The invitation presupposes that an inner voice is God's, but it is not clearly offered as public proof replacing the preceding arguments. E751–E758 later make experiential entitlement conditional on the absence of defeaters.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The warning against concentrating exclusively on arguments does not explicitly override contrary evidence. The later allowance for delusion or error at E751–E752 prevents treating this as unconditional immunity.",
      "emotionalDevices":["comfort"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"An invitation to attend to religious experience alongside argument, rather than to disregard objections."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":311,"endEvent":312,"contextStartEvent":302,"contextEndEvent":340,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"I just believe in one less God than you do. And that's really a small difference.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E307–E310 supply the numerical comparison. Here it introduces common ground and B's position; it is not used to establish that the remaining deity does not exist. B subsequently explains his evidential standard at E328–E340.",
      "protectionExplanation":"No criticism is excluded, and E337–E340 explicitly leave open what religious belief might survive examination.",
      "emotionalDevices":["identity"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A memorable introductory comparison intended to reduce social distance between believers and atheists."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":328,"endEvent":328,"contextStartEvent":313,"contextEndEvent":340,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"An atheist is simply a person who demands good reasons for all beliefs",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"unclear","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"The definition associates atheism with a generally admirable intellectual standard. It can lend identity-based credibility before particular arguments are examined, but E337–E340 frame the judgment as provisional and E382–E385 promise substantive examination.",
      "protectionExplanation":"It does not say that all disagreement proves irrationality or that religious arguments cannot succeed; E372–E375 expressly allow success.",
      "emotionalDevices":["identity"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A description of the kind of evidential atheism B intends to defend, rather than an exhaustive psychological description of atheists."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":407,"endEvent":409,"contextStartEvent":387,"contextEndEvent":410,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"In a weird sort of way, if all of them can claim to be true, none of them can be true.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"yes","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E393–E406 give reasons why unfalsifiability alone supplies no evidential advantage. The core wording goes further: competing claims to truth are made to yield that none can be true, a step those reasons do not establish. E774 and E1815 later use the weaker conclusion that they cannot all be true.",
      "protectionExplanation":"This is an overextended inference, not an explicit rule neutralizing all possible objections or evidence.",
      "emotionalDevices":["ridicule"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"An imprecise way of saying that none earns acceptance merely by claiming immunity from disproof."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":528,"endEvent":529,"contextStartEvent":497,"contextEndEvent":529,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"the atheist wins because the more reasonable position is the conservative position, stick with what you know.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"unclear","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E511–E527 offer an analogy from scientific expansion and acknowledge speculative status. The maxim supplies a decision rule for a claimed stalemate. It supports withholding additional belief, but its adequacy for concluding that only nature exists remains disputed at E966–E1077 and E1657–E1683.",
      "protectionExplanation":"B does not exclude future supporting evidence for supernaturalism; E372–E375 allow a sufficiently strong argument to succeed. Preference for a conservative hypothesis alone is not immunity.",
      "emotionalDevices":["comfort","identity"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"An economy-of-belief rule for suspending commitment to unsupported additions, not a deductive proof of their nonexistence."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":545,"endEvent":546,"contextStartEvent":531,"contextEndEvent":546,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"The atheist doesn't want to live in the dark, finding it more reasonable to live in the light.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E536–E544 explain the target: an imagined theology that accommodates both favorable and unfavorable conditions. The light/dark affirmation summarizes that criticism. Those imagined responses must not be attributed to A as adopted claims.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The passage criticizes a purported protective move in another view; it does not itself establish an unrestricted dismissal of any supernatural evidence.",
      "emotionalDevices":["identity","ridicule"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A rhetorical summary of a methodological preference for claims that can gain or lose evidential support."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":582,"endEvent":583,"contextStartEvent":577,"contextEndEvent":583,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"These things are culturally relative and have no bearing on what reality is ultimately like.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"unclear","protection":"unclear",
